strengths: The paper proposes a complete architecture containing both learning-based and classic map-based planning methods to improve the performance on the visual object navigation task.
The two approaches are combined using a decision module.

Navigation is performed either by choosing actions based on a reinforcement learning pipeline fed by semantic segmentation of the scene, or by classical map-based navigation actions achieving both exploration and goal reaching.

In the case of visual based navigation, the proposed method exploits the advantages of SegmATRon to achieve more reliable segmentation of the scene via online modification of the segmentation model weights during inference by using a buffer of frames collected during the execution of the actions.
The authors do a good job of performing ablations of their own method to determine the relative contribution of each of the components of their pipeline.
The diagrams of their proposed pipeline are well made and clear.
The description of the approach is presented clearly and the motivation and details are explained well.
The paper presents a valid and reasonable system for the ObjectGoal Navigation task.
Experiments show some improvement over baselines.

The authors propose an interesting approach for object navigation that outperforms the baselines. Because it uses both classical map-based approaches and learned approaches, it is able to leverage the best of both worlds.
Approach is robust to segmentation noise.
Writing is generally clear with a few gaps here and there (see below).
The proposed approach outperforms the baselines on a recent object navigation challenge, though the improvement is marginal under the OneFormer setting.
Ablation study is useful. We can see how different parameter setups affect performance (e.g. number of frames, agent turn angle).
weaknesses: The writing quality of the paper and the use of English could be improved.
The paper suffers from a tight page limit, resulting in brief descriptions of the full model and individual modules that do not cover crucial details regarding motivation and design choices.
It is very hard to reproduce this work based on the paper content, as many details regarding the architecture and the parameters of each module are not provided.
The proposed architecture appears to be heavily based on the SkillFusion paper, including a more powerful semantic segmentation approach (SegmATRon), but this is not clearly stated in the text.
A detailed comparison between the SkillFusion model and the presented SkillTRon model is missing.
A comprehensive comparison with corresponding state-of-the-art methods should be provided to clarify the relative improvement and contributions of the proposed work.

The experimental results have substantial errors: SkillTron+SegmATRon is evaluated on a manually selected subset of validation episodes from the HM3D dataset, while the comparison numbers from the Habitat Challenge are from a completely different, non-public test set, leading to inaccurate comparison against published state-of-the-art methods.

The authors should evaluate SkillTron+SegmATRon on the full HM3D test set and compare against other papers that use this standard public test set, or submit to the Habitat Challenge to obtain results on the same secret test set, ensuring reproducible evaluation.

The claim of “significant improvement” over SkillTron+OneFormer is unsupported, as the changes in success rate, SPL, and SoftSPL are 0.02 or less in every case and no standard error metrics are reported, making it unclear whether the semantic map method yields a statistically significant performance change.

Many statements throughout the paper compare to related work but are conjectures stated as facts, such as the claim that “such approaches are not correctly linked to the algorithms for planning map trajectories” regarding (Ramakrishnan et al., 2022).
The authors should consider motivating their method: if the goal is to find a highly accurate semantic map, they need to explain why highly performant semantic SLAM methods are not used.
The paper writing needs significant improvement for both English and the writing flow. I cannot understand a lot of sentences. And I can barely read into understanding the paper details.

The paper is more like an experiment report after participating the Habitat ObjectGoalNav challenge than a paper. The problem formulation is very specific for the specific challenge. I'm not sure if the paper has any generality that makes it interesting for general ICLR paper readers.
The proposed system mostly uses previous works as its components. It's unclear if there is any technical contribution in the method.
Experiments are weak, only comparing to 2 team submissions.

The motivation for the work is not very clear. Why do we think it's necessary to have the 4 combinations: classical exploration, classical goal reaching, RL-based exploration, RL-based goal reaching? What's the benefit over having just classical or just RL?

Writing is generally clear with a few gaps here and there, such as the definition of L_{fusion}, or when RL-based exploration is used (it is in Fig. 2 but not mentioned in Sec. 4.1 Skill Fusion Decider).

Navigation Image Sequences in 4.2 is not very well motivated. Is it to generally increase prediction accuracy by providing more contextual information about the scene/visuals? It's not clear how this relates to the segmentation model being trained on offline data.
Very similar to SkillFusion (Staroverov et al.). The contributions over this prior work seem minor.
